overview: Atropatene was a kingdom in northwestern Iran, distinct from Greater Media and from modern Azerbaijan. This map shows only 323 to 200 BCE, not its full political lifetime. Its exact ancient boundaries remain uncertain. The nearby Karafto caves and the later Avroman documents discussed below fall outside the imported outline; they illuminate the wider frontier region, not securely identified royal possessions.

periods.title: Atropates and his successors
periods.summary: A regional dynasty developed after Alexander’s death.

periods.title: An agreement with Antiochus III
periods.summary: Artabazanes accepted a treaty favorable to the Seleucid king in 220 BCE. The map stops in 200 BCE.

items.text: Atropates had served the Persian king Darius III before Alexander reinstated him as governor of Media. After Alexander died in 323 BCE, the northern portion remained with Atropates while Greater Media went to another governor. This separation helped create a durable regional kingdom.

Royal family connections mattered. In 324 BCE, just before this map begins, Atropates’ daughter married Perdiccas at Alexander’s great wedding celebrations at Susa. Her marriage linked the governor’s household to one of the most powerful Macedonian commanders.

In 220 BCE Antiochus III advanced against the elderly ruler Artabazanes after suppressing Molon’s rebellion. Artabazanes made a treaty favorable to Antiochus. Political survival could mean negotiating with a stronger neighbor while preserving a local ruling house.

sections.title: Water, herds and finding ancient towns

items.text: Water helped determine how people earned their food. Kroll’s regional archaeological gazetteer describes cultivation around Lake Urmia and along rivers where sufficient water was available, and pastoral herding in other areas. Farming and looking after animals belonged to the same varied landscape.

Rain and snow made winter and spring journeys difficult. Kroll consequently places much ancient travel in summer and autumn. A family or trader preparing a journey had to think about the season as well as the destination: the mountains did not provide an all-weather timetable.

Even identifying a royal city can be detective work. Kroll regards Leilan as a probable location for Ganzak, but stresses that Phraaspa’s location is much less certain. Archaeologists also face difficulty separating remains from successive Iranian empires. A large ruin does not arrive with a convenient ancient address label.

sections.title: Karafto: a nearby frontier cave complex

items.text: At Karafto, just outside this map’s southern outline, people carved rooms into cliffs and adapted natural caves. Von Gall describes two main levels and a southern entrance roughly nine metres above the ground. The complex preserves substantial human workmanship, although the date of each alteration is not equally secure.

Some rooms have barrel-shaped ceilings. Doors in rooms k and l could be barred from inside, while the window lintel in room k imitates wooden construction in stone. These details bring practical concerns such as closing a room into view, without establishing who slept there.

The cave’s purpose is debated. Von Gall considers communal feasting or meetings, alongside sacred uses; other scholars have proposed a garrison. Its limited lookout weakens a straightforward guard-post interpretation. Carved rooms and a religious inscription alone cannot settle whether this was a residence, sanctuary or mixed-use gathering place.

A doorway carries Greek writing dated by its letter forms to the late fourth or first half of the third century BCE. The second line reads “μηθὲν εἰσέλθοι κακόν” (mēthen eiselthoi kakon), “May nothing evil enter.” The preceding line names Heracles. This is a protective wish, not a royal proclamation or proof that everyone nearby read Greek.

Robert Ker Porter recorded the inscription in 1819. Its survival above an entrance lets researchers study writing in its architectural setting, rather than as an object with its original location lost. The protective formula also occurs in ordinary buildings elsewhere in the Greek-speaking world.

sections.title: Later regional life, after the map ends

items.text: Writing around the beginning of the Common Era, Strabo describes the dynasty’s marriages into Armenian, Syrian and Parthian royal families. This later account makes family relationships part of diplomacy. It also shows why Atropatene should not simply be renamed Armenia or Parthia when its rulers formed alliances.

Strabo also describes the salts of Lake Capauta, identified with Lake Urmia, as irritating the skin, and reports olive oil as relief. This is a glimpse of an ancient account of bodily discomfort and a remedy. It does not document a medical school or a system of public healthcare.

A later vineyard contract from Avroman names a buyer, Gathakes, and two brothers selling property, Barakes and Sobenes. The British Library dates it to either 88 or 24 BCE, depending on the calendar era used. This document comes from outside the mapped outline, in the wider Median region, and reveals a particular family transaction.

The Avroman parchment puts Greek on one side and a short Parthian text on the other. Its Greek deed appears twice, with differences between the versions. A sealed portion could protect a text while another remained readable. Ancient paperwork had its own way of making unauthorized changes harder.

The Avroman documents were found in a jar in a cave in 1909. Czajkowski explains the double-document method: if the accessible version was disputed, the sealed version could be opened for comparison. This evidence concerns legal writing; it does not establish how children in Atropatene were taught to read.

ending.text: Atropatene did not disappear when this map stops in 200 BCE. It later came under Parthian supremacy while retaining local institutions; the timing of that change is uncertain. Arsacid princes eventually replaced the earlier dynasty, and the region entered the Sasanian realm in the early third century CE. These were changes of political authority, not the disappearance of its inhabitants.
